From that moment on, G. with his family, his parents, and two brothers-in-law with their families had disappeared from the village. Where they are is unclear. In the weeks after the attack, the municipality, under police escort, entered the sealed-off grounds on Ewijkseweg twice more. According to someone in the know, G.'s girlfriend was allowed to briefly return during one of those visits to collect essential items, such as identity documents. The house reportedly had been completely turned upside down during several police investigations. The animals that stayed on the grounds, including horses and large guard dogs, have been placed in boarding facilities. Arrest in Germany. On 18 September G. was arrested in Germany at the request of the Dutch authorities. He is suspected of involvement in the import of cocaine via the port of Dunkirk. According to German police, he was travelling towards the Netherlands via the A44 motorway from the direction of Saxony-Anhalt. Since then G. has been held in a German cell. He still speaks with his lawyer from time to time, but meanwhile a court case looms in Den Bosch. There he will have to answer for his involvement in the cocaine case surrounding Dunkirk, on top of all the other problems that are dogging him. Interviews with those involved. This story is based on a large number of conversations that the authors conducted over the past five weeks with people directly involved in the Overasselt case. All conversations were held on the basis of anonymity. Information from other sources and from official bodies was also used.

title: 18.000 chickens dead in large fire in Zeeuws-Vlaanderen
lead: A very large fire raged this afternoon in a chicken barn in Biervliet in Zeeuws-Vlaanderen. The 18.000 chickens did not survive the fire, a spokesperson for the safety region confirmed to Omroep Zeeland. The fire released a lot of thick, black smoke that could be seen from far away. The Veiligheidsregio Zeeland (VRZ) warned residents to keep windows and doors closed. Cause unknown According to the regional broadcaster, it concerns an organic laying hen barn. The fire broke out around 15.00 hours. The cause is still unknown. There were no people present in the barn. Three fire engines were deployed to fight the fire. A crane is also being deployed to break open the barn. Around 16.30 hours the fire was reported under control. The fire brigade will still be busy for some time extinguishing remaining hot spots.

title: Injured in attack on airport in Saudi capital Riyad, air traffic at a standstill
lead: An unknown number of people have been injured in attacks on the international airport in the Saudi capital Riyad. Two regional officials say the airport has been evacuated after a missile hit a passenger terminal. According to witnesses, ambulances were rushing to the airport. All air traffic to and from King Khalid International Airport has been halted. A source at a local hospital told news agency AFP that dozens of people were injured in the attack. He saw gate 401 of the domestic terminal being hit. "I saw the injured with my own eyes. Everyone ran away." Data from Flightaware shows that at least 225 flights at King Khalid International Airport have been cancelled in the past 24 hours, following the earlier attacks on the airport this week. The airport calls on travelers to contact their airline and check the status of their flight before coming to the airport. Several airlines have already taken measures. Kuwait Airways cancelled all flights to and from Riyad today. Several embassies in Riyhad, including the US embassy, have called on their citizens to avoid the international airport and the surrounding area. Yemen The attack comes two days after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked the airport in Riyad. Three Saudis lost their lives in that attack, including a pilot. That international airports are targeted in a series of attacks is exceptional. Earlier this week the Houthis also attacked airfields in the Saudi towns of Jizan, Najran and Abha. These lie a few tens of kilometers from the border with Yemen. Saudi Arabia supports the Yemeni government army, which is fighting the Houthi rebels. Since the start of the large-scale Operation Dawn of Yemen by the Yemeni army last Monday, the Houthis have stepped up their attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia. The European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) has tightened its guidelines for Saudi airspace. It points to the Houthis' ability to hit targets deeper in the kingdom, including Riyad, and to their "greater focus on aviation infrastructure". The missile and drone attacks, as well as the attempts to intercept them, "increase the risk that civil aircraft will be hit", the agency says. Under fire Meanwhile, the fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces continues. Saudi Arabia is providing air support to the internationally recognized government in Yemen in an attempt to reverse the Houthis' recent territorial gains along the Red Sea. Because of the situation in Yemen, some 200,000 people have fled, including to Djibouti, a small country in the Horn of Africa. The UN migration and refugee agency (IOM) called on countries this week to take action. Saudi Arabia has sought support from the US and other allies, now that its airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure are under fire. This concerns, among other things, sharing intelligence and planning and identifying targets. 'I am not happy' When the American president Trump left the White House yesterday, he was asked about the attacks on the airport in Riyad. "It is not good" and "I am not happy", he told reporters. For now there are no signs of American military support in response to the attacks. The ministers of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> of Saudi Arabia and Oman spoke by phone this week about the importance of "support for diplomatic solutions to reduce tensions in the region". Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, regularly acts as a mediator. But there is not yet any prospect of a solution to the escalation.

title: Municipalities want more money for resilience against disasters and threats
lead: Municipalities feel they are receiving too little money from the national government to make themselves resilient against all kinds of threats. These include, for example, cyber and hybrid threats or dangers arising from climate change, such as nature fires. <entity id="person:sharon-dijksma">Sharon Dijksma</entity>, chair of the Association of Netherlands Municipalities (<entity id="org:vereniging-van-nederlandse-gemeenten">VNG</entity>), says that for the resilience task municipalities need several times what is budgeted in the Miljoenennota. "I assume that in total it really is a matter of hundreds of millions." "<entity id="org:kabinet">Het kabinet</entity> has earmarked 35 million for emergency support points and now, in the Miljoenennota, has added a gradually increasing series of 20 to 70 million for digital resilience, socio-societal resilience and continuity alike. But the gap between what municipalities need and what the cabinet is making available is therefore large," says the VNG. <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">Rotterdam</entity> also wants more money. The Rotterdam port is often cited as a possible target for threats from Russia. "Resilience goes further than emergency support points, after all. We must also invest in society itself, in a strong social fabric that helps us during an emergency and in the recovery afterwards," says a spokesperson for the municipality. No evacuation facilities. The VNG already has a fairly clear picture of how municipalities would like to deploy extra money. "You can think of neighbourhood emergency plans and training for residents. We still need to talk with the ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-justitie-en-veiligheid">Justitie en Veiligheid</entity> about sheltering and evacuation, for which there are now almost no facilities." "Emergency generators, satellite phones and pagers are needed, and the emergency services need many more resources, such as fire engines. The list is too long to list everything." VNG chair Dijksma, who is also <entity id="pos:burgemeester-utrecht">burgemeester van Utrecht</entity>, does have an idea of what needs to happen in her municipality. "We have many vulnerable residents who are not self-reliant, and they do not always have the money to prepare. We also need money for communication tools that we still lack." In Austerlitz, a village in the <entity id="org:gemeente-zeist">gemeente Zeist</entity>, people do not want to wait until municipalities have sufficient resources for safety exercises. Austerlitz lies in the middle of the forest and has few access roads. Because residents feared they would not be able to get away properly in the event of a major forest fire, volunteers set up a 'forest fire working group'. Today the volunteers of the working group practised as if a major forest fire was raging: "I am part of the group of citizens who keep an eye on everything when there is a risk of nature fires," says Robert Schliessler. "We work together with the safety region and train for what happens when our village is threatened." Today Schliessler is also taking part in the first exercise together with the safety region. "We have a WhatsApp group in the village, with six hundred people in it, and they will all be told there when the exercise begins. We have been asking the safety region for this exercise for three years and are super happy that it is finally here," he adds. "By now we work well together with the municipality and the safety region." The idea is that the group of volunteers keeps a close eye on 112 reports and passes on to residents that evacuation is needed. "We do that earlier than the emergency services. We have three locations where people can find each other, and these are determined at the moment we know where the fire is." 'Cannot be financed'. Dijksma is very positive about the exercise in Austerlitz. "It is very important that people also prepare themselves; these kinds of initiatives are gold." Municipal resilience falls under the Ministry of Justice and Security, and <entity id="person:david-van-weel">Minister Van Weel</entity> is also pleased with the initiative. "I am glad that challenges are being identified and that these kinds of things are being picked up and improved locally." Van Weel can certainly follow the call of the municipalities for more money. "In the Miljoenennota we have designated resilience as an important theme, but our spending will not cover all wishes," he says. "It is an enormous task, so I am not going to say we can do everything at once. We cannot finance that." According to the minister, municipalities can certainly get to work with the money they already receive, for example to work on the resilience of their critical processes. "Ultimately, resilience lies in the communities where people live; municipalities have a very large role in that."

title: Until at least 23.00 no trains between Rotterdam and Delft after arson
lead: No trains will run between Rotterdam and Delft until at least 23.00. The reason is the arson last night at a railway bridge in Rotterdam-Delfshaven. ProRail does not rule out that sabotage is involved. According to the railway manager, it will take until at least Sunday evening before the damage is repaired. Trains may not run on the route again until Monday morning. The railway between Rotterdam and Delft is one of the busiest routes in the Netherlands. It is also used by trains covering long distances, for example between the Randstad and Zeeland or Limburg. For train travellers, this also means a lot of inconvenience tomorrow. Eight-hour check According to ProRail, it is certain that the fire was deliberately started last night. The fire started last night in the technical room. The door to it had been pried open and inside lay smouldering cables. Research shows that 35 cables were damaged. Fifteen of them have burned through completely and must be replaced and re-welded. After replacing all cables, various checks must be carried out to determine whether the trains can run safely again. These checks take about eight hours. Whether sabotage was actually committed on the railway again must still be investigated by the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> and fire brigade. No one has been arrested yet.

title: From our correspondent... Boris van der Spek (Central America)
lead: Van onze Correspondent is a series by the makers of the podcast De Dag. Every Sunday we get to know one of the NOS correspondents, the country where they live and the stories that, in their view, deserve more attention. Today: Boris van der Spek, correspondent in Central America. Listen here: You can listen to this episode of De Dag via <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> Luister and all other podcast apps. Do you like it? Then don't forget to subscribe. After studying journalism, Boris moved to Latin America. After a trip in his youth, he wanted to go back there. And he had long dreamed of becoming a correspondent on that continent. Methodically, he ticked off the ingredients needed to become a correspondent: speaking the language, having been there once, and falling in love. After meeting his current wife, Boris moved to Chile. There he worked as a correspondent for the first time and set up his own news outlet. Eventually the Chilean <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> visited his in-laws after he had written a story. "That made me very angry." After eight years he had had enough of Chile: "You want to do more, but newspapers were not waiting for a story from the country every week". Chaos. And then there was Mexico. "A wonderful chaos," Boris said. You have to be careful, with the drug cartels calling the shots in some places. "Fields are full of mines, there are ever heavier weapons on the streets. And that's just Mexico, you know, you're not in a war zone." But the Mexicans Boris meets are warm, invite him to stay for dinner and to sleep over, and teach him a lot about life. "I find how Mexicans deal with death very inspiring. Through rituals and ceremonies, my late mother stays alive." Going back to the Netherlands is not an option for now: "That would be too great a culture shock". Boris would rather stay for years more on the continent of his dreams: Latin America. Next week in our series: Van onze correspondent Mustafa Marghadi, the correspondent in Southeast Asia. Do you have a question for him? Email dedag@nos.nl Presentation & editing: Marco Geijtenbeek Editorial: Wouter Sloekers

title: Northern lights visible in parts of the Netherlands (but only through a camera)
lead: Between the rain showers, the northern lights could be seen last night and overnight. At least, through a lens. The so-called photographic northern lights cannot be seen with the naked eye, but a camera can capture them. Especially in the southern half of the country, people had a chance to capture the northern lights. There was less cloud cover there than in the north. Via NOS Ooggetuige, photos of the natural phenomenon came in from Limburg, South Holland and Gelderland. The colourful glow is caused by a solar storm: an eruption of electrically charged particles from the sun. Energy is released in the process, resulting in the play of colours in the sky. Northern lights, also known as aurora borealis, were regularly visible in the Netherlands in recent years because there was maximum solar activity then. That will be less in the coming years, so the chance of seeing it is smaller. "In the quiet period, around 2030, the chance of seeing the northern lights in the Netherlands is very small", says the <entity id="org:koninklijk-nederlands-meteorologisch-instituut">KNMI</entity> .

title: Widespread outrage over attack on Riyadh airport: 'Dangerous escalation'
lead: The attack by Houthi rebels on the airport of the Saudi capital Riyadh is being widely condemned internationally. World leaders speak of a deliberate attack on a civilian target and call it a dangerous escalation of the fighting on the Arabian Peninsula. Twelve people died and more than 300 were injured when the passenger terminal was hit yesterday afternoon. It is thus the most serious attack on a Saudi target since fighting in Yemen flared up again halfway through this year. Earlier this week the airport was also hit by an attack from Yemen. Only limited footage of the attack is available because Saudi Arabia has strict censorship. Anyone who shares footage of attacks or damage may face a severe penalty. Several embassies have therefore advised their nationals not to post or forward footage. Nevertheless, some footage of the attack came out: UN envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg calls the attack a serious escalation. "These kinds of actions pose a serious threat to regional security, perpetuate a cycle of violence and hamper the search for peace in Yemen." UN chief Guterres calls the attack on a civilian target a violation of international law. "This must stop immediately." Canadian Prime Minister Carney also says that "there is no justification whatsoever for attacks on civilian infrastructure". For the Netherlands, <entity id="person:tom-berendsen">minister Berendsen</entity> of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> condemns the attack. "The Netherlands stands in full solidarity with the people of Saudi Arabia and our Gulf partners." Retaliation A Houthi spokesperson has claimed responsibility for the attack in a statement to The New York Times. According to him, it is direct retaliation for Saudi attacks on his country in which civilians died. According to his count, 91 people have died since 3 September, mainly women and children. "The world must understand that airports, ports, weddings, funerals, hospitals and markets in Yemen are civilian targets that you should not attack," he reasons. "That applies both to Yemen and elsewhere." American interference? The American president Trump, in a conversation with journalists, did not want to say whether American armed forces would support Saudi Arabia's fight against the Houthis. The US carried out several attacks on the Houthis shortly after Trump took office last year, but recently turned down Saudi requests for support. "Who knows, we will look into it," Trump answered evasively when asked whether he was reconsidering his position. "We have only just heard of the recent attack, so we will still have to decide. We will do so quickly." He called the attack on the airport "terrible". Analysts pointed out earlier that the US is now focused mainly on the conflict with Iran and therefore is not waiting for a second front in the region. Moreover, the American weapons arsenal is said to already be depleted by the attacks on Iran and the defence against counterattacks from that country. Tirade over Nobel Prize: After his short answer about the crisis in the Middle East, Trump took longer to lash out at the Norwegian Nobel Committee over its choice of jurist Navi Pallay. He once again repeated his incorrect claim that he had ended eight wars, freed hostages in Israel and prevented a conflict between China and Taiwan. "I've stopped eight wars and then they give the Nobel Prize to someone nobody has ever heard of. I had never heard of her, nobody I know had ever heard of her," Trump said. "Something is wrong in Norway, I can tell you that." Trump has in the past made no secret that he himself would like to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Recently he said that "the US, with me as its representative, should have received the Nobel Prize". That this did not happen he called an "indelible stain" on Norway's reputation.

title: Rainbow flag flown across the country, flags stolen in Oldebroek
lead: The much-discussed rainbow flag flies at <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. The flag was raised in connection with Coming Out Day, a day on which there is extra attention worldwide for coming out. It is the first time the rainbow flag hangs at the representative body. Flags have also been hung throughout the country, but in the Gelderland municipality of Oldebroek several rainbow flags have been stolen. The municipality decided this week to scrap its LGBTI policy, and therefore also not to hoist a flag. That decision led to much discussion in the municipality. In protest, residents of Oldebroek hung up flags. At the Kruiskerk in the municipality, a rainbow flag was raised yesterday in the presence of dozens of people. 'Colourfulness' According to Reverend Han Wilmink, the flag is in fact a Christian symbol. "It shows the colourfulness of God's creation and everyone belongs to that. We will not leave anyone aside here." The residents' action soon met resistance: on Saturday evening it became clear that several flags had been stolen, including the flag at the church. De Stentor reports that some flagpoles were even vandalised. Meanwhile a new flag hangs at the church. How the issue is playing out in Oldebroek (and divides the municipality) you can read here: In <entity id="org:gemeente-alblasserdam">Alblasserdam</entity> tempers also ran high. There the flag was already flying two days ago. The hoisting was not announced in advance. The municipality then published a post on social media with the text: "In Alblasserdam there is room for everyone". Swastikas were placed under the post, the local paper writes. In addition, people called for the flag or the flagpole to be removed by force. The comments under the post have since been disabled. Vote on the flag. In the Tweede Kamer the hoisting of the flag led to much discussion. The presidium, the daily board of the Tweede Kamer, first decided to hoist the rainbow flag. But after opposition from the Christian opposition party the SGP, that plan did not go ahead. Other opposition parties then however submitted a motion to nevertheless have the flag hoisted on Coming Out Day. On Thursday evening a vote by roll call was held, after which it became clear that a majority of the House wanted to have the flag flying next to the parliament building after all.

title: Governments cherish oil refineries due to high fuel prices
lead: High prices at the pump and an impending diesel shortage are leading to a different view of the future of the oil refineries in Rotterdam and Vlissingen. Although the oil era is coming to an end due to climate policy, petrol, diesel and kerosene are still needed for now. Governments want to prevent production capacity from declining faster than demand for oil products. Europe currently depends partly on imports from abroad for diesel and kerosene. Because of the war in the Middle East, businesses and consumers are paying record prices for these. The European Commission wants to get rid of this dependence. President Von der Leyen therefore announced this week a "strategic dialogue" on refineries in Europe: "The goal is to lower costs and to have enough stocks, also for defence." Earlier, NATO Secretary General Rutte already warned of a shortage of diesel for tanks and kerosene for combat aircraft in a possible war situation. Next week, climate minister Stientje van Veldhoven will present the plans for the future of refining in the Netherlands. Key position in Europe. The Netherlands plays a very large role in the production of petrol, diesel and kerosene. The refineries of Shell, BP and ExxonMobil in Rotterdam and the Zeeland Refinery in Vlissingen produce tens of billions of litres of fuel for the European market. This summer they made somewhat more kerosene because of shortages in aviation; at the moment somewhat more diesel is being made again. The costs of producing fuels are higher in Europe than in other parts of the world. This is partly due to the price of CO2 rights that companies must buy in order to be allowed to emit greenhouse gases. In addition, electricity costs in the Netherlands are higher than in neighbouring countries and it is difficult to get a heavy grid connection. The challenge for <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> is now to ensure that refineries that will ultimately have to disappear keep producing optimally in the short term. At the same time, CO2 emissions must be reduced further. In addition, faster progress must be made on developing sustainable alternatives to diesel and kerosene. This concerns, among other things, green hydrogen and biofuels. The largest refinery in Europe is Shell's in Pernis. Every day just over 400,000 barrels of crude oil are converted into fuels here. A year ago Shell cancelled the construction of a bio-refinery for sustainable diesel and kerosene, even though more than half a billion euros had already been invested in it. The reason was competition from Asia and an insufficient blending obligation for biodiesel and bio-kerosene, according to the company. Five years ago Shell already produced the first synthetic kerosene in its laboratory for a KLM flight to Madrid. This sustainable aviation fuel is made from green hydrogen and CO2. According to Shell, the market for synthetic fuels is not yet ready for mass production. That does not mean nothing is happening in Rotterdam. Shell has built the first large factory for green hydrogen in the Netherlands. The Finnish Neste produces biofuels on the Tweede Maasvlakte and is currently doubling production to 2.7 million tonnes per year. The Dutch company Power2X is working on a factory for synthetic kerosene. The location lies exactly between the refineries of Shell and Exxon Mobil. Profits in the billions. To emit less CO2, Shell and Exxon Mobil are taking part in capturing and storing CO2. The greenhouse gases from the refineries are then partly stored in an empty gas field under the North Sea. In the coming years, capturing and storing CO2 will further increase the costs of refining. Building new oil refineries is not an obvious choice given the approaching end of the oil era. Shell has already more than halved the number of refineries worldwide in recent years. The Gunvor refinery in Rotterdam was closed last year. To maintain sufficient refining capacity in Europe, costs must not deviate too much from those on other continents. Because so much fuel is made in Rotterdam and Zeeland, other European countries are also looking at the Netherlands. Limiting costs for refineries is not uncontroversial. The oil giants are currently making billions in profits every quarter because of high fuel prices. The environmental movement will not thank the minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-kgg">Klimaat en Groene Groei</entity> if support comes for the production of diesel and kerosene.

title: Renewed flooding in Nepal, five people missing
lead: Five people have gone missing in a new flood in Nepal. A landslide near the village of Chumnubri sent debris into the Budhi Gandaki river, which led to a flood. According to Nepalese authorities, two women and three men are missing. 49 people were rescued, including a foreigner. So far there have been no reports of fatalities. The flood also caused major damage: at least thirty houses and two suspension bridges were swept away. A construction site of a hydropower plant was also hit, and part of the construction material has been carried away by the river. In these images the force of the water after the landslide is clearly visible: Evacuation Villagers living downstream along the river have been called on to leave their homes and move to safer places. The army, the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> and other rescue workers have been sent to the flood area. The situation is being monitored by helicopter, Nepalese authorities say. The Budhi Gandaki river flows into the Trishuli river. A huge ice avalanche caused a devastating flood there in August. The wave of debris, mud and water swept through the disaster area at speeds of over 180 kilometres per hour. More than 1,300 people died and more than 5,000 people are missing. The Nepalese government now assumes that they are also dead. You can read here how the flood wave in the Trishuli river came about: Weeks after the disaster, the missing were still being searched for, but last week Nepalese prime minister Shah announced that the search would be ended. This caused mixed feelings among the bereaved. Some want the Nepalese government to keep searching for their loved ones, and held demonstrations for that. Others were glad with the decision; they could now apply for a death certificate. According to an estimate by the Nepalese government, the reconstruction of the area will cost well over 4 billion euros.

title: Deaths in bus crash in Turkey
lead: Eleven people have been confirmed dead in a serious bus crash in Turkey. Another 27 people were injured. The coach crashed on the slip road of a motorway between the cities of Bursa and Izmir, in the west of the country. It is unclear exactly what went wrong. Footage shows the bus lying on its side. Next to it lies a lorry loaded with wood. That lorry has also overturned. The Turkish minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> confirms the death toll on X. He says emergency services have been deployed in large numbers to help at the scene of the accident.

title: Utrecht struggles with how to deal with unscrupulous landlords and looks to Rotterdam
lead: Overdue maintenance, discrimination and far too high service charges: landlords in Utrecht regularly break the rules for good landlordship. Yet fines mostly fail to materialise. The municipality is now considering taking stronger action against abuses in the rental sector and is looking to Rotterdam for this. To protect people against, for example, excessive rent or intimidation by the landlord, there is the Good Landlordship Act. This came into force in 2023 and was expanded in 2024. This law stipulates that municipalities may act against rental abuses. Tenants must first report a violation to the municipality. Rent reduced by 350 euros Rotterdam issues fines more quickly than Utrecht for violations. In 2025 Rotterdam imposed 25 fines or orders subject to a penalty payment on landlords. The fines range from 1000 euros to several tens of thousands of euros per violation. That year there were also dozens of investigations into abuses. In that year Rotterdam received 667 reports. The threat of a fine alone seems successful: in many cases the municipality reached agreement with the landlord. After reports of excessive rent, the amount has, according to the municipality of Rotterdam, been reduced by an average of 350 euros. First a warning Utrecht imposed one fine in 2025, RTV Utrecht reports. According to the municipality, this is partly because residents do not always dare to report abuses. In 2025 the municipality received 197 reports. "Many tenants, given the tight housing market, are already glad to have a home and do not want to risk jeopardising their housing situation," the college writes. This municipality further chooses to first give landlords a warning. Not yet decided The municipality will now investigate whether it can adopt Rotterdam's approach. The college thinks fines can be a deterrent and prevent repetition. A decision has not yet been made. The municipality wants to avoid being overturned by the court because the imposed sanction is too severe. The municipality does, however, aim to introduce a rental permit in 2028, whereby the rent can be checked in advance. Furthermore, Utrecht wants to better inform tenants about their rights and about the reporting point where abuses can be reported.

title: Man arrested in Poland for planning an attack on Prime Minister Tusk
lead: A man has been arrested in Poland for preparing an attack on Prime Minister Tusk, reports Marcin Kierwiński, the Polish minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>. The identity of the suspect has not been made public. It has also not been disclosed what the background is or how the suspect would have intended to carry out the attack. Tusk thanked the police for their "swift and decisive action". Earlier it became known that Polish security services had convened an emergency meeting after information about a possible attack on Tusk and Minister of Defence Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz. The Polish authorities did not go into detail, but the threat was taken "extremely seriously". The chance that the attack would actually be carried out was described as high. The report of the attack threat came in by email this morning at the state security service, the Ministry of Interior reports. Radical organisation: Polish broadcaster TVN24 says it has seen the content of the email. According to the broadcaster, the person who reported the threat had contact via social media with a radical organisation. That organisation was reportedly looking for people who wanted to carry out attacks with firearms. The person who reported the threat is said to have come into contact with a man with whom he spoke about weapons, hatred of the government and plans for mass murder, TVN24 writes.

title: Where fear gives way to hope: more tourists to the predominantly Kurdish Diyarbakir
lead: In the southeast of Turkey, heavy fighting between the Turkish army and the Kurdish PKK was still taking place eleven years ago. Today there is renewed hope for peace. In recent years it has become quieter, and since the peace process between <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity> and the PKK began, the region is even being promoted to give tourism a boost. You see more and more residents from different parts of Turkey travelling to the southeast and thus discovering their own country. And not without reason, according to a visitor from Istanbul: "Diyarbakir is the Paris of the East". A region that was largely isolated for years now seems cautiously to be stepping into the foreground. Among residents and business owners, fear is giving way to hope. "You can of course never say 100 percent that something will never happen again," says tour guide Berkay Ozbilge. "But hopefully it won't happen." The predominantly Kurdish Diyarbakir is built at a crossroads of cultures. September and October are popular months to visit the city in the southeast. It is therefore busy in the historic centre. Diyarbakir has an enormous amount to offer, says Serdar Baturay, who has worked in the tourism sector for 21 years. "There is religious heritage from various faith communities, but there are also the historic city walls and the Hevsel Gardens, which are on the Unesco World Heritage List." Millions of tourists. The goal is five million tourists in 2032. According to Turkish media, in the first eight months of this year 1.3 million tourists from within and outside the country visited the city. Among them are also Turks from Northern and Western Europe. A Turkish Dutch woman who is visiting with her husband tells NOS: "It is a city with a rich history and that appeals to us a lot. We also find the people here very friendly." For some visitors a trip to Diyarbakir is extra special. "I was born here, but I haven't been back for 18 years," says a woman on the street. During the years of unrest in the region she did not dare to return. "That's why I find it quite exciting now." The Turkish Dutch woman visited Diyarbakir earlier, in 2018, after a very turbulent period and heavy fighting. "We already felt safe then, but it feels more familiar now." The peace negotiations have, according to her, a positive effect on the city. You can see that on the street, she says. Fighting in 2015: In 2015 Diyarbakir was still the battleground for fighting between the Kurdish PKK and the Turkish state. Large parts of city neighbourhoods were destroyed. Thousands of people fled. Now it is quiet in the city again. The Turkish government and the PKK have been negotiating for peace for some time. That was preceded by a bloody struggle of at least forty years, in which 40,000 people lost their lives. The loss of loved ones still leaves deep scars in many families. The peace process is therefore seen as an important step. Still, residents have concerns about whether these negotiations will lead to lasting peace and more rights for the Kurds. That is also because in the past, peace talks came to nothing. 'It's all behind us' Meanwhile, many residents appreciate the current calm and long for economic stability. A shopkeeper in the historic centre explains that there are still people who are afraid to come. "They think everyone here carries a weapon. That's how they know this place. Whoever has never been here and has not seen it with their own eyes doesn't know what it is really like. But when they come here and see it with their own eyes, they say: 'Oh, how beautiful it is here'." Tour guide Berkay Ozbilge, who has a bus full of tourists in sight, says: "After people have seen the nightlife of Diyarbakır, all those prejudices disappear. Just like in Istanbul, nightlife in Diyarbakır and in the eastern region simply goes on. Street bans and curfews, the order to stay home; that time is over. It's all behind us."

title: Scheveningen beach closed for some time: 'sea mine' turns out to be harmless steel ball
lead: Last night, hours of investigation took place in Scheveningen into a washed-up ball that was feared to be an old sea mine. In the end it turned out to be a harmless steel ball. Footage shows how the Explosive Ordnance Disposal service of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-defensie">Defensie</entity> went to work: The metal ball washed up on the beach around 15.00 hours on Sunday. Passersby alerted the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>, which closed off the beach with several units. That cordon was later widened to keep onlookers at a distance. The Explosive Ordnance Disposal service Defensie (EOD) then came to Scheveningen to examine the object. In the end it turned out not to be a sea mine. The police report that it may be an old buoy.

title: One dead and eleven injured in new attack on Riyadh airport
lead: In a new attack on Riyadh airport yesterday, one person was killed and eleven people were injured. The General Authority of Civil Aviation of Saudi Arabia (GACA) reported this in a statement. It was the fourth attack on the airport in five days. The person killed was of Pakistani nationality. The injured have been taken to hospital. The attack also caused material damage, the extent of which is still being assessed, GACA reports. Last Saturday, the airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh was also attacked. Thirteen people were killed and more than 300 injured, some of them seriously. It was the deadliest attack in a Gulf state since the start of the war between the US and Israel with Iran in February. Risk of further escalation. Much remains unclear about the damage at the airport. There is little footage, and spreading it carries heavy penalties. Security plays a role in this, but censorship is in any case strict in many Gulf states. Yesterday, Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Media did release footage of the first attack: The Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport increase the risk of further escalation, although Saudi Arabia is not seeking this, experts say. However, the expectation is that the country will strike back hard, which could in turn lead to new attacks back and forth. The new attack on Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis reported that the airport in Sanaa, the capital of Yemen, held by the rebels, had been attacked again. Al-Masirah, the television station controlled by the Houthis, reported further attacks on Sanaa. According to the rebel group, Saudi Arabia is behind them. That country has not yet responded to the attacks on Yemen. Attack in Dammam too. Saudi authorities also reported an attack on King Fahd airport in Dammam on Sunday. An eyewitness aboard an aircraft told news agency Reuters that a projectile struck near parked aircraft there on Sunday evening, after which a fire broke out. The attack on the airport in Dammam has also been confirmed by GACA. The American aviation authority FAA has urged US airlines to be cautious with flights to or over Saudi Arabia because of security risks. This warning remains in effect until 10 December. The European aviation authority EASA already tightened its advice for airlines on 9 October after an attack on Riyadh airport. For Dutch travellers, the <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">ministerie van Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> has issued an orange travel advisory for most of the country since 8 October. This means travellers are advised against travelling there unless necessary. A red travel advisory applies to the border area with Yemen, where all travel is advised against because it is too dangerous there.

title: Two dead and two injured in traffic accident Kesteren
lead: Two people were killed and two others injured in a serious accident on the N233 near Kesteren last night. The accident happened shortly before 23.00 hours. Dagblad De Gelderlander reports that the fire brigade, six ambulances and two trauma helicopters were called out. One of the cars ended up upside down in the verge. The driver of that car is one of the fatal victims, according to the newspaper. The N233 between the A15 and Kesteren will remain closed for the coming hours.

title: Explosion at hairdresser in Vlaardingen, possibly linked to 'hairdresser war'
lead: In Vlaardingen, an explosion took place at a hairdresser's shop last night around 23.00 hours. The explosion caused damage to the facade. A shop window was completely blown out. The cause of the explosion has not been announced. Photos show a piece of heavy fireworks and a loose brick. There have been more incidents involving hairdresser's shops in Vlaardingen. Regional broadcaster Rijnmond and the AD reported last summer about a so-called 'hairdresser war' in the South Holland municipality. The hairdresser's shop on Westhavenkade had also previously been the target of vandalism. Bricks were thrown at the shop window at that time, Rijnmond reported. The reason for the attacks is unclear, but it is being speculated that they could be related to unfair competition. The hairdressers who are targets are said to be charging prices for haircuts that are below the usual rates, the AD wrote earlier this year.

title: How to defeat Russia? NATO's top military officer answers in a rare speech
lead: How does NATO defeat Russia if that country attacks the military alliance? The alliance's military commander gives the answer this afternoon at a security summit in Warsaw. The announcement of his speech promises nothing less than a 'theory of victory' over the Russians. Because the title reads: 'The theory of victory: how do we achieve military success against Russia through deterrence and defence?' According to news site Bloomberg, the speech says that NATO wants to swiftly repel a Russian attack with artificial intelligence and large quantities of drones. Ground troops should also be deployed to stop an invasion and destroy the Russian command structure. Speech live on NOS The speech by the American Supreme Allied Commander of NATO, General Alexus Grynkewich, can be followed live from 13.00 via the NOS app and NOS.nl. NOS correspondents Kysia Hekster (NATO) and Christiaan Paauwe (Central and Eastern Europe) explain in the stream what makes the speech so special. The speech comes at a tense moment. European countries increasingly see 'hybrid attacks' which are suspected to be the work of the Russians. Those attacks are also becoming more serious. They include arson at ammunition depots with weapons for Ukraine, sabotage on the railways, armed or unarmed drones appearing, and hacks. Western security services see the number of attacks increasing very rapidly. Panic is the goal The attacks aim to sow panic and reduce support for Ukraine. For NATO it is difficult to respond to this kind of attack that is not 'serious' enough to strike back fully, as intended in the famous Article 5 of NATO ("an attack on one is an attack on all"). Moreover, it is often difficult to prove that the Russians are indeed behind them. Meanwhile a discussion has broken out about the term 'hybrid attacks'. "We must stop that," says, for example, the foreign minister of Estonia. According to him, these are terror attacks and sabotage attacks that amount to 'a kind of war'. At the headquarters in Brussels there is restraint. We must not let ourselves be provoked, keep a cool head and continue supporting Ukraine, is the thinking. Still, it now seems time for a public NATO answer to the Russians. It comes from the mouth of NATO's military commander Alexus Grynkewich, an American four-star general. As well known as NATO chief <entity id="person:mark-rutte">Mark Rutte</entity> is, the military commander, in jargon Saceur, an abbreviation of Supreme Allied Commander Europe, is usually that anonymous. The highest operational commander of the alliance is always an American, the political head a European. Speech especially remarkable That the Saceur is seeking out the media today makes it especially remarkable, says Eleonora Russell, former head of communications of NATO's military branch. She thinks it is good that Grynkewich is coming out into the open. "Such a widely announced, strategic speech his predecessors never gave. But Grynkewich is different. He says: if I don't speak out, the chance of war increases. He has good relations with the White House. What he is going to say has Trump's support." In this way the alliance also hopes to show that the American president is "fully committed" to NATO, as Rutte keeps emphasising. Trump himself often sows doubt about his involvement. For example, he said that NATO countries that do not contribute enough to the alliance could, in his view, be attacked. This week he also concluded an agreement with President Putin for the import of large quantities of diesel oil, intended to bring down pump prices before the mid-term elections in America. According to the British newspaper Financial Times, the American president also threatens to halt weapons deliveries to Ukraine through a NATO programme if that country continues attacking Russian energy facilities. Cooperation, not deterrence These are examples of cooperation with Moscow instead of deterrence. Yet this afternoon's speech must reassure NATO countries and make clear that the alliance is ready to strike back if necessary. According to Russell, this 'theory of victory' is not NATO's first, but it is a first that it is partly presented at the request of the allies. In Moscow and Beijing the speech will undoubtedly be listened to with interest. But is it wise to put such a NATO playbook with all the ins and outs out into the open? "He of course will not do that," says Russell. She thinks Moscow will use the story regardless as 'proof' that the alliance is out for war. The speech will emphasise exactly the opposite: NATO is a defensive alliance that responds to an attack. Deterring the Russians is the purpose of the theory of victory, so that it never has to become practice.

title: D66 wants lower threshold for speaking with child when child abuse is suspected
lead: Governing party D66 wants children to be spoken with quickly when there are serious signals of child abuse, where necessary without consultation with the parents. That is stated in a private member's bill by MPs <entity id="person:marijke-synhaeve">Marijke Synhaeve</entity> and Hanneke van der Werf. The proposal is being published online today so that organisations can respond. "What we want is for children to be better heard, seen and helped", says Synhaeve. In recent years it became clear in serious cases that the child was not heard. Examples are the girl who was tortured in Stadskanaal and the foster girl in Vlaardingen, who was also seriously abused. In both cases, signals from the children or their environment were not picked up properly. Specialist bodies such as the Children's Ombudsman have long been calling for the voice of the child to be heard more when abuse is suspected. Only now after parental consent. MP Synhaeve says she has spoken with many victims who said they were not listened to. With the 'child-first law', the MPs want to ensure that children get help quickly and do not have to tell their story to many different people. Most importantly, they can be heard without parental consent if the parents may be involved in the abuse. Currently, care providers may in principle only make contact with the child if the parents or guardians give consent. Only under strict conditions can this be deviated from. But this is complicated and does not happen often. Barnahus-model. The bill states that the method can be used when there are signals of criminal offences. The approach is to apply to children both within and outside youth care. Within 48 hours a special team must hear the child and come up with a plan for protection, care and, where necessary, criminal prosecution. The team involved must consist of people with different areas of expertise in medical care, youth care, safety and justice. This approach is based on the Barnahus-model, which is already used in many other countries. Barnahús is Icelandic for 'children's house'. It is a child-friendly, multidisciplinary approach for child victims and witnesses of violence, sexual abuse or exploitation of children. Better cooperation. Synhaeve is not worried that the approach will lead to much extra work or more out-of-home placements. According to her, it will instead lead to agencies cooperating better and help being available more quickly for children and families who need it. Once the responses from organisations are in, the bill, possibly in amended form, will be submitted to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>.

title: Bricks without gas kilns? Full power grid stands in the way of more sustainable industry
lead: Many regional industrial companies cannot make their operations more sustainable. For the production of glass, cardboard and stone, for example, they often use large machines that consume a lot of energy. In the coming years these must be replaced, and companies would preferably do so by switching to electric machines. But there is too little room on the power grid. That is stated in the report by Cluster6, a partnership of regional energy-intensive industrial companies in manufacturing, waste processing and the Ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-kgg">Klimaat en Groene Groei</entity>. The brickworks of the company Wienerberger are also affiliated with the partnership. Some 70 million bricks and paving stones are made there each year, still largely with the help of gas kilns. But if it is up to director Jasper Vos, those will quickly become electric appliances. One of the factories is on the waiting list for a heavier power connection. "We were promised that there would be room somewhere before 2030, but the question is whether that will actually happen," he says at the location in Pannerden, north-east of Nijmegen. Grid congestion First of all, why is there not enough capacity on the power grid? That is because in recent years companies and households have switched to electricity to a great extent, but the underground cables were not designed for that. This creates grid congestion; in the morning and evening demand for power is much higher than during the day and at night. The grid operator takes these 'peaks' into account and therefore cannot grant every new request. In any case, not before the cables can handle it. Therefore grid operators are reinforcing the power grid. The Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets introduced measures two years ago to resolve shortages on the power grid. This means that socially important institutions such as schools and hospitals get priority on the grid. Companies that help reduce grid congestion, such as solar and wind parks or companies installing large batteries, also get priority on the waiting list. Industrial companies end up at the very bottom of the waiting list. Interim solutions Because the waiting list is tied to a region, companies in a region where there is little 'competition' on the power grid may get a connection immediately, while companies elsewhere have to wait for years. "Take for example a glass factory that wants to become sustainable in 2030. If the grid operator tells it that there is only room in 2034, the factory has to bridge that gap," says Barbara Verwayen, who represents the regional industrial companies on behalf of Cluster6. According to her, temporary, local generation of electricity at the companies could offer an interim solution. "If that can be done sustainably, then that is terrific, with sun, wind and batteries. If it cannot be done sustainably, we will have to temporarily generate extra electricity with gas turbines." In this way companies could, while waiting for a heavier power connection, still start investing in electric machines. But more is needed for that than money alone, says Verwayen. "Laws and regulations, the legal framework, granting of permits, all those things." Resistance Grid operators have been working on reinforcing the power grid for some time. To do so, they are building around a hundred high-voltage stations and other power infrastructure in the coming years. Finding a suitable location is often complicated. Protected flora and fauna or proximity to a Natura 2000 area can make building a new station impossible. In addition, operators often encounter resistance from local residents who would rather not see an industrial high-voltage station in their 'backyard'. This causes delays and uncertainty about the expansion of the power grid in the Netherlands. "Due to uncertainty about a power connection, investments are leaking away abroad," says Vos of the Wienerberger brickworks. "You look over the river here to Germany. Similar companies in neighbouring countries do have access to electricity. If we do not get that certainty and space, the survival of this type of company in the Netherlands is at stake."

title: Strike in Belgium over cuts to public services: fewer trains, VRT also on strike
lead: In Belgium, trade unions are protesting again today against announced cuts by <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity>. The strike day will affect schools, public transport and waste collection. Staff at the Flemish broadcaster VRT are also laying down their work. The strike is an initiative of the socialist union ACOD. The protest is aimed at the cuts to public services announced by the regering-De Wever. Tomorrow the prime minister was due to explain the budget choices in his State of the Union, but due to the absence of a budget agreement that has been postponed. His government has been in crisis since this weekend, because the coalition parties cannot agree on that budget. Rail: The strike at the Belgian railway company NMBS began yesterday evening and until 10.00 p.m. this evening fewer trains will run. This also affects train travel to and from the Netherlands, NS reports. Travellers are advised to check the journey planner before departure. Fewer buses, trams and metros are also running in Belgium. Staff at broadcaster VRT are also laying down their work. The broadcaster still has to cut 10 million euros, on top of an earlier announced round of cuts. Many TV broadcasts are being scrapped, news bulletins have been shortened and on the radio there will mostly be music, the broadcaster reports. On 9 November a decision will be taken on further actions. Riots: Last Friday a strike in Brussels against cuts to social security ended in riots, after hundreds to thousands of masked youths had mixed in among the demonstrators. They threw stones and fireworks at the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. The police said the disturbances were not linked to the union action. At least 110 people were arrested. A day earlier a ban on gatherings was announced in Liège, because of education protests that had got out of hand in that city. Those protests have partly spilled over from France, where since last month demonstrations have been held against, among other things, the poor state of school buildings and the teacher shortage.

title: Crash between crane and bus causes havoc in Nijmegen
lead: In Nijmegen a bus was damaged this morning in an accident with a crane truck. A passenger was injured and taken to hospital, Omroep Gelderland reports. The accident happened this morning around 07.00 hours on the Industrieweg, on the western edge of Nijmegen. While braking for a roundabout, the ballast of a crane truck hit the side of a bus carrying passengers. An advertising column and several lampposts along the road were also struck. Several emergency services, including several officers and an ambulance, went to the scene. A bus passenger who was sitting at the back of the bus was taken to hospital by ambulance staff. The other passengers were transported to Nijmegen by smaller buses. Havoc The collision caused havoc. A large part of the Industrieweg towards the centre of Nijmegen is strewn with debris from the advertising column, lampposts and glass. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> is investigating the cause.

title: SPD leader Bas steps down after attacks from coalition partner CDU in 'difficult time'
lead: Bärbel Bas, co-chair of the German governing party SPD, has unexpectedly stepped down. She also gives up her post as minister of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-sociale-zaken-en-werkgelegenheid">Sociale Zaken en Werkgelegenheid</entity>. The departure follows a death in the family and ongoing attacks on her personally. "After the death of my stepdaughter I realised I need more time to process the grief", Bas writes in a statement. Precisely in this "personally difficult time" the attacks on her have increased, she continues. "Also from the ranks of our coalition partner." According to the other co-chair, vice chancellor Lars Klingbeil, boundaries have been crossed. The attacks are "unseemly" and "poison the political culture", he says. "I am worried that we are losing empathetic figures in politics." Women in particular are targets of such attacks, hatred and incitement, according to Klingbeil. Bas belonged to the heart of the German government, but as minister repeatedly clashed with federal chancellor Merz and his CDU/CSU. The Christian Democrats want to reduce social contributions and regularly came up against Bas, who belongs to the left wing of the social democratic SPD. When Merz claimed that the current welfare state is unsustainable, Bas spoke of "bullshit". In recent weeks the CDU/CSU criticised Bas for the slow implementation of controversial pension plans, which are unpopular within the SPD. Bas would have deliberately slowed the reforms, while it was known within the coalition that there was a death in her family. Sour relationship The attacks on Bas are heavily criticised by SPD members. "The attacks by the CDU, despite her personally difficult situation, were inhumane and reckless", writes the influential SPD member Manuela Schwesig, state premier of Mecklenburg-Voor-Pommeren. Party colleague Bernd Rützel speaks of unacceptable attacks, both by CDU members and by "certain media". Within the CDU/CSU, Bas's outburst is in fact seen as inappropriate. Focus Online writes that the parliamentary group stayed away from criticism precisely because of her situation. An insider told the news site it was a "cheap kick when she is down". According to the Süddeutsche Zeitung, Merz did complain about Bas's absence, including to journalists. It shows how sour the relationship between the governing parties has become. Both parties feel the other is obstructing agreed reforms. Merz recently blocked the planned sugar tax, a project of SPD vice chancellor Klingbeil. On the other side, the SPD has objections to pension reforms. The election of a parliamentary president from the radical right-wing AfD in the state of Saksen-Anhalt, with the help of CDU votes, also led to tension. The SPD demands an explanation of this and wants the coalition partner to act against those who voted for it. Conversely, the CDU is pressuring the SPD not to govern with Die Linke in the state of Berlin, a party that the Christian Democrats consider antisemitic. Negotiations on healthcare reforms became so tense that federal president Steinmeier had to intervene, because he feared the government would collapse. Both parties, however, have no interest in a coalition break-up or new elections. The CDU/CSU in particular has fallen into free fall in the polls in recent weeks. Merz critic as successor Bas's ministerial post will be taken over by Alexander Schweitzer, former premier of the state of <entity id="org:waterschap-van-rijnland">Rijnland</entity>-Palts. In the past week he openly criticised Merz, who "does not deliver" and governs with a "cold neoliberal spirit of the 1990s". He also sneered that the CDU does not convincingly support Merz. With Schweitzer in this important post, the government once again has an SPD member who takes a critical stance towards the CDU's reform plans. At the same time there is little room to tinker with the agreements already concluded. It is now up to federal chancellor Merz to keep the squabbling coalition together. After the defeats in recent state elections, there was much speculation about his resignation. He stayed on, but with diminished authority within the party. He has tied his fate to carrying out the reforms. The party leadership met today to discuss how the CDU should proceed. Later today Merz will hold a press conference on this.

title: Dismissed dentist drives into dental practice in Belgium out of revenge
lead: In Belgium a dismissed dentist drove his car into a dental practice out of revenge. The driver was slightly injured. He was taken in by police for questioning. According to the Flemish broadcaster VRT, the Romanian man drove his Porsche through the rear of the building in Stekene in East Flanders at around 22.30 hours last night. The driver drove through the glass entrance door of the waiting room, put the car in reverse and then drove into the practice once more. The rear of the building was badly damaged. It took hours for the fire brigade to clear the damage and close the windows and doors. VRT reports that the man worked at the practice but had been dismissed. Nothing has been made public about the reason for his dismissal.

title: Cabinet wants to make it easier for zoos to improve enclosures
lead: There must be new rules for zoos, believes <entity id="person:silvio-erkens">staatssecretaris Erkens</entity> of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-landbouw-visserij-voedselzekerheid-en-natuur">Landbouw, Visserij, Voedselzekerheid en Natuur</entity>. Zoos that want to renew now face too many extra rules and permits, he believes. Whereas zoos that leave everything as it is have no trouble at all, precisely because they do not innovate. "Zoos have been a beloved outing for young and old for ages", writes Erkens in a letter to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. "At the same time, over the years we have come to attach more value to animal welfare. It is therefore important that zoos keep up with the times." At the moment zoos still have permits for an indefinite period. Only zoos that want to innovate face new tests and the associated costs. A zoo that never changes anything can go on for years without running into rules. Erkens wants to change that. No flexibility Animal care manager Tjerk ter Meulen of zoo Artis in Amsterdam cites as an example the stones in an aquarium. For a permit application, all of them must be marked on a floor plan, including size and weight, he says. "That gives us no flexibility to change them again when the fish need it. Of course we want to constantly respond to the needs and welfare of the animals. And if we then have to apply for a new permit for the enclosure every time, that of course makes things very difficult."

title: Misconduct reported at Utrecht nursing home: 'She simply hasn't been showered for a year'
lead: Relatives of residents of a care centre in <entity id="org:gemeente-utrecht">Utrecht</entity> sound the alarm with RTV Utrecht about the conditions on a nursing ward. They say residents are poorly cared for and often left to their own devices. The psychogeriatric ward of Nieuw Tamarinde in Overvecht houses around twenty elderly people who have some form of dementia. Nieuw Tamarinde is part of care institution Careyn. It is active in the municipalities of <entity id="org:gemeente-stichtse-vecht">Stichtse Vecht</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-de-ronde-venen">De Ronde Venen</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-woerden">Woerden</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-oudewater">Oudewater</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-montfoort">Montfoort</entity>, Utrecht and Zeist. RTV Utrecht spoke with several relatives of residents, who wish to remain anonymous. They describe the problems that are occurring on the ward. For example, there is said to be poor care, a lack of hygiene and problems with administering medication. According to the relatives, staff are often nowhere to be seen. 'Not showered for a year' Two women describe the lack of care for their aunt: "She stank at one point. Her nails were very long and there was faeces under them. She was wearing dirty clothes, greasy hair and no mouth care had been done." RTV Utrecht has viewed the aunt's file. Staff members write in it how the woman is doing and what they have done. For example, a carer writes on 4 May this year that "madam" has not been showered for a year because she "resists". The plan is now to wash the woman with two people from now on, so that she can resist less. "She simply hasn't been showered for a year," says her niece indignantly. "She would not have wanted that." 'My mother's dentures were stuck fast' Another woman describes the situation with her husband. "I went there every day. At 9.30 he would be sitting in his wheelchair with greasy hair and black nails," she says. "Then they would pay attention to it and then it would go well for a while." According to a fourth woman, her mother's dentures are not being cleaned. "Her dentures were stuck fast," she says. She describes how a staff member forcefully pulled the dentures out of her mother's mouth. "Her dentures hadn't come out for months." Temporary agency staff The relatives have complained several times to Careyn's management, but so far, they state, little has changed. "It goes well for a bit when you say something about it, and then it's wrong again," says one of them. Careyn's management acknowledges the problems and attributes them to staff shortages. In a complaints mediator's report it can be read: "Every time people drop out again, which partly undoes the improvements." Many temporary agency workers work on the ward, and according to the relatives that is where the problem lies. "A number of permanent staff are really very kind and good, but they are often not there," says a relative. Inspection reports Care institution Careyn informs RTV Utrecht in a written response that it is aware of the relatives' concerns and says it has taken measures to improve the situation. "We have also organised family evenings to listen to what is going on, to discuss concerns and to look together at what needs to be better." The care institution acknowledges that "things have not gone well". "The measures we have put in place have not yet led to the improvement that is needed on all points. We must also face that." The <entity id="org:inspectie-gezondheidszorg-en-jeugd">Inspectie Gezondheidszorg en Jeugd</entity> tells RTV Utrecht that seven reports have been received since the beginning of 2025. The inspectorate cannot say anything about the content of the reports or who made them. The inspectorate does not want to say whether an investigation into the ward will follow.

title: New arrests for fatal shooting incident at Vierdaagsefeesten Nijmegen
lead: The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> has arrested two new suspects in the investigation into the fatal shooting during the Vierdaagsefeesten in Nijmegen. They are a 19-year-old man from Amsterdam and a 21-year-old man from Hoorn. On Tuesday 21 July, at around 22.00 hours, an 18-year-old man from Rotterdam was shot dead on Graafseweg. This happened not far from the Vierdaagsefeesten, which were underway in the city at that moment. That same evening, an 18-year-old fellow city resident was arrested. He was released again a day later and has not been a suspect since, reports Omroep Gelderland . The police have since investigated the shooting incident and what preceded it. "This has now resulted in two arrests", the police report. The men are suspected of involvement in the shooting incident. The motive for the shooting is still being investigated. The police therefore are not currently sharing any further information about what the two are specifically suspected of.

title: Minister Hermans scraps 13-week scan for pregnant women from 2028
lead: Pregnant women will no longer be able to use a 13-week scan from 1 January 2028. The current experiment with the scan to detect congenital abnormalities will not be continued, Minister Hermans of Health writes to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. Last month the <entity id="org:gezondheidsraad">Gezondheidsraad</entity> advised against introducing the 13-week scan as a standard part of maternity care. The results of the scan did not always turn out to be correct; sometimes women were referred unnecessarily, while relatively many abnormalities were missed. The Gezondheidsraad concluded that the benefits do not currently outweigh the disadvantages. Hermans largely follows that advice, but goes one step further than the Gezondheidsraad. The council had still argued for further research to use the scan in such a way that the benefits would outweigh the disadvantages. But the minister is not keen on that. Unnecessary anxiety. "Although <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> takes the possibilities for improving the protocol seriously, there currently also appear to be many disadvantages to offering the 13-week scan again within a research setting", writes Hermans. She especially does not want to expose pregnant women again to unnecessary anxiety if the result turns out to be a false alarm. That means the 13-week scan will disappear on 1 January 2028. The research has been offered since 2021 as part of a scientific study, alongside the usual 20-week scan. The idea behind it was that parents with a scan in the thirteenth week of pregnancy have more time to prepare for a child who needs a lot of care or for a possible abortion. In her letter to the House, Hermans writes that she does want to examine the entire chain of prenatal screening. In doing so, she wants to look at how the current system, with scans and the NIPT blood test to detect genetic abnormalities, can be improved. If scientific developments give cause for it, she may ask the Gezondheidsraad again for advice on the 13-week scan.

title: Rail staff talk about suicide: 'standing talking to her for 1,5 hours'
lead: Start the conversation: that is the message of a new campaign for suicide prevention on the railways. Each year around 200 people die in the Netherlands in a collision with a train. Attempted suicides are far more common still. Train drivers, conductors and ProRail employees are now speaking out with their stories in a campaign by 113 and the railway companies. In this way they hope to contribute to reducing the number of suicides. NS head conductor Glenda (41) "I have now been head conductor for 8,5 years. In that period I have experienced one suicide and found perhaps twenty suicidal people. On the tracks, around the station, on the platform. Sometimes it happens very often in a row, sometimes not at all for a year. The first time I experienced it, we received an emergency call 'suicidal person'. After we had stood still for twenty minutes, we got permission to drive again. We were about two kilometres on our way when the driver paged me: 'There is someone in front of my train, can you come forward?' The driver said: 'She is a very young girl, maybe it is better if you go outside.' I then climbed out of the train. She was standing right in front of the train, with her arms wide, and shouted very loudly: 'Make sure he drives, make sure he drives.' I talked to her for about an hour and a half. Eventually she climbed into the train, we drove on and handed her over to the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. I have learned to recognise behaviour that is not understood, for example when it is very cold outside and someone is standing there in a T-shirt. I also now know how to deal with it. Do ask that direct question about suicide. If you are off the mark, someone will understand that it was asked with the best intentions. During rush hour I once saw a person standing completely still. Everyone walked around them. Something in me said: this is not right. I went over to them and took them out of the crowd. I did not go into their world until I asked: 'Are you here because you wanted to jump in front of the train?' Then I pulled her out of that daze and she said: 'Yes, that is what I came here to do.'" Incident responder at ProRail Dennis Heijne (34) "We are alerted to animals on the tracks, but also to people with behaviour that is not understood. When there is a collision we receive an alert. As team leader I then select the men and women who make sure the passengers of NS or Arriva can continue as quickly as possible. The number of collisions I have experienced is already getting close to 190. I always find the number a bit confronting to mention. And we have not even got to near-collisions or people around the tracks. You have to be able to deal with that, be able to hold conversations. Otherwise you cannot do this job. We are retrained several times a year. How can you share things? How do you talk about 'I'? It also happens several times a day that we prevent suicides. Then we can make sure people get the right help, if it has not yet been started. It may be that someone with behaviour that is not understood is seen on ProRail cameras, or by bystanders. We then go looking straight away, together with the police. To start a conversation, I first say who I am: Dennis from ProRail. Then I look for something to talk about, which can be something simple: 'I see you have an iPhone.' I want to make a connection, to get someone out of the danger zone. To a bench, away from that level crossing." 113 Are you thinking about suicide or worried about someone? Talking about it helps and can be done anonymously via the chat on www.113.nl or by phone on 113 or 0800-0113.

title: EU countries hold off on a hard response after US sanctions against the Court
lead: The European Union is for now choosing the diplomatic route to keep the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague standing. Harsh measures against the American sanctions against the court are not coming for now. That is the outcome of a meeting of the ministers of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> of the EU countries in Luxembourg. "The most important thing is to engage in dialogue and do everything to protect the court," said <entity id="person:tom-berendsen">minister Berendsen</entity> of Buitenlandse Zaken after the meeting. Belgium would have preferred to take a harder stance against the American sanctions, but does not get sufficient support. Last Friday the American government announced sanctions against the Court. The US is an opponent of the ICC. It does not recognise the court and demands that the ICC not prosecute American nationals. The arrest warrant against Israeli prime minister Netanyahu also led to great anger among Americans. After the sanctions take effect next April, it will be prohibited for American citizens, companies and organisations to do business with the ICC. Organisations outside the US also face sanctions if they cooperate with the court. Earlier, sanctions were already imposed on individual judges and prosecutors at the International Criminal Court. Unacceptable The EU countries called the sanctions unacceptable on Friday. They did stress, however, that the six-month period before the sanctions take effect still offers the chance to engage in talks with the United States. Belgium called today for doing more than just talking by now instructing companies to ignore the American sanctions. European rules offer that possibility. The Netherlands, like the majority of EU countries, wants to keep that option in reserve, partly out of fear that the conflict with the Americans over the Court will otherwise escalate, with possibly major financial consequences for companies. According to Belgian minister Prevot, a firm signal is precisely needed because some companies that now work with the Court are "preventively withdrawing their support." Minister Berendsen could not confirm that this is actually happening. He does see that there are concerns among companies. He therefore finds it important to engage in talks with companies, and to show "that they have full support to continue their work for the court". Red line? In the coming months it will become clear what negotiations will yield. The Americans want the court to no longer be able to prosecute American nationals. Experts stress that such a concession would jeopardise the functioning of the court. "If you grant immunity to residents of one country for the most serious international crimes, then you not only undermine the functioning of the court, but the entire international legal order," said professor of International criminal law Marieke de Hoon on Friday to Nieuwsuur. According to minister Berendsen, the independent functioning of the court is of crucial importance. Whether the American demand is therefore a red line he does not want to say, however: "It is not up to the Netherlands to determine what we can and cannot grant. That is up to the more than 120 countries that are affiliated with the Court". Greenland deal The hope is to still be able to convince the Americans in the coming months to lift the sanctions, without the functioning of the court suffering as a result. In Brussels the Greenland deal is mentioned as an example of how the Americans could still come round. Meanwhile, preparations are also continuing in case the Americans do actually impose the sanctions. In the coming months the countries that participate in the International Criminal Court will use the ICC to protect it as much as possible against the sanctions. They want to do this, among other things, by working with companies and banks that have no ties to the US at all. At an EU summit later this week in Brussels, the heads of government of the member states will also discuss the American sanctions with each other.

title: Other (online) supermarkets are busier due to problems at Albert Heijn
lead: Due to the problems at Albert Heijn, other supermarket chains are busier. A spokesperson for Jumbo says that chain is already scaling up. Jumbo already sees an increase in online orders. The company cannot yet say whether more people are also coming to the stores because shelves are empty at some Albert Heijn branches. "We have to anticipate higher demand.
